What we do: The company maintains information security policies that define security roles, responsibilities and requirements. Policies are approved by management and reviewed at least annually.
Evidence: Policy set; approval and version history.

Control: Management review of the security programme
What we do: Management reviews the status of the security and compliance programme at least semi-annually, and decisions and actions are recorded.
Evidence: Review notes or minutes with date, attendees and actions.

What we do: The company maintains an organisational chart that shows reporting lines, and updates it as the structure changes.

Control: Code of conduct and disciplinary policy
What we do: A code of conduct sets out expected behaviour and the disciplinary process for breaches.
An acceptable use policy sets out how personnel may use company systems, devices and data.
Personnel acknowledge the code of conduct and information security policies when they join and at least annually.
Evidence: Acknowledgement records for new and existing personnel.

Control: Oversight of automated and agent-run controls
What we do: Each automated or agent-run control has a named owner. Failures and exceptions are escalated for human review, and changes to the control's logic or permissions are approved before use.
Evidence: Automation inventory with owners; exception queue; change approvals.

What we do: Background checks are performed on new personnel before they start, where permitted by law.
Evidence: Background check results for new hires.

What we do: Personnel complete security awareness training when they join and at least annually.
Personnel and contractors sign confidentiality agreements before they are given access to company systems.
Personnel receive a performance evaluation at least annually.
A risk management policy defines how risks, including fraud risk, are identified, assessed, treated and monitored.
A risk assessment, including fraud risk and changes to the business, is performed at least annually and recorded in the risk register.
Each identified risk has an owner and a treatment decision, and residual risk is accepted by management.
Evidence: Risk register with owners, treatments and acceptance.

What we do: The control framework maps controls to risks and requirements, and is reviewed at least annually and when the business or systems change.
New vendors are assessed and approved before they handle company or customer data, and a central vendor inventory records each vendor's data access and criticality.
Critical vendors and subservice organisations are reviewed at least annually, including their independent assurance reports and the complementary controls the company must operate.
Evidence: Assurance reports; review records; CUEC mapping.

What we do: Agreements with vendors that handle customer data include security, confidentiality and, where relevant, data protection terms.

The company documents the controls it relies on from {{cloud provider: Amazon Web Services (AWS)}} and reviews its independent assurance report at least annually, including the complementary controls the company must operate.
Access to in-scope systems is requested, approved by the manager or system owner, and provisioned centrally before use.
Evidence: Access requests and approvals; user listings with creation dates.

What we do: Access to in-scope systems is removed within one business day of a person leaving the company.
Joiner, mover and leaver events in {{HR system: Rippling}} trigger account creation, changes and removal, and HR records are the source for access reviews and leaver checks.
Evidence: HR event reports matched to account changes.

What we do: User access to in-scope systems is reviewed centrally with system owners at least quarterly, and inappropriate access is removed.
Access to in-scope systems is granted by role, based on least privilege.
Privileged access to production is limited to authorised personnel, and the list of privileged users is reviewed at least quarterly.
Multi-factor authentication is required for access to in-scope systems.
Access to in-scope systems is federated through {{identity provider: Google Workspace}} using single sign-on wherever the system supports it.
{{identity provider: Google Workspace}} enforces an authentication policy that requires multi-factor authentication for all users.
Personnel store and share credentials in {{password manager: 1Password}}, the company's password manager.
Each user has a unique account for in-scope systems, and shared or service accounts have a named owner.
{{cloud provider: Amazon Web Services (AWS)}} root and break-glass accounts are protected with multi-factor authentication, are not used for routine work, and their use triggers an alert.
Evidence: Root account MFA; alert rule; usage log.

Control: Staff access to customer data (exception only)
What we do: Staff access customer data only for an approved support or incident case, and each access is recorded against the ticket or customer request.
Network traffic to production is restricted by firewall rules or security groups that deny by default, and rules are reviewed at least annually.
Evidence: Firewall or security group rules; review record.

Control: No public access to data stores
What we do: Production data stores and administrative interfaces are not accessible from the public internet.
Data sent over public networks is encrypted using current TLS.
Customer data stored in production is encrypted at rest.
Application secrets and encryption keys are stored in {{secrets manager: AWS Secrets Manager}}, access is restricted to authorised services and people, and keys are rotated at least annually.
Evidence: Secrets and key access policies; rotation history.

What we do: Public traffic to the production application passes through {{edge protection: Cloudflare WAF}}, which enforces encrypted connections and web application firewall protection.
{{database: Amazon RDS}} production databases use encryption at rest and in transit, private network access and unique database users.
A data classification and handling policy defines data types and how each must be protected.
Customer data is logically segregated by tenant in the application and data layers, and segregation is tested at least annually.
Evidence: Data model; penetration test scope and results.

What we do: Company devices are enrolled in {{device management: Kandji}}, which enforces disk encryption, screen lock, OS updates and the company's configuration baseline.
Policy: POL-09 Asset and Endpoint Security Policy

What we do: Anti-malware protection (built-in OS protection is acceptable) is active on company devices, checked at least quarterly.
Policy: POL-09 Asset and Endpoint Security Policy

What we do: An inventory of devices and production assets is maintained and reviewed at least annually.
Policy: POL-09 Asset and Endpoint Security Policy

What we do: Devices and media holding company data are securely wiped or destroyed before disposal or reuse.
Policy: POL-09 Asset and Endpoint Security Policy

What we do: {{infrastructure scanner: Amazon Inspector}} scans production infrastructure for vulnerabilities at least weekly, and findings are tracked to remediation.
{{code scanner: GitHub Dependabot}} scans application code and dependencies on every change to production code, and findings are remediated within defined timeframes.
Critical and high vulnerabilities are remediated within defined timeframes, or risk-accepted by management.
An independent party performs a penetration test of the production application and infrastructure at least annually, and critical and high findings are remediated and retested.
{{cloud configuration monitoring: AWS Security Hub}} continuously checks production cloud configuration against a security baseline, and findings are triaged and remediated.
{{audit logging: AWS CloudTrail}} collects audit and security logs from production systems and retains them for at least one year, with access restricted.
{{threat detection: Amazon GuardDuty}} monitors production for security threats, and alerts are routed to responsible personnel who triage and resolve them.
Evidence: Detection configuration; alert history and triage notes.

What we do: An incident management policy defines how security events are identified, classified by severity, escalated and resolved.
An incident response plan defines shared roles across security, operations and engineering, with a named incident lead for each incident, and is reviewed at least annually.
Incidents are recorded, tracked and resolved by severity, and affected customers are notified in line with contractual commitments.
The incident response plan is tested at least annually through a tabletop exercise or a real incident, and lessons are acted on.
A change management policy defines how changes are developed, reviewed, tested, approved and released to production.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Application code is kept in {{code repository: GitHub}}, and branch protection prevents direct changes to production branches.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Each change to production code is reviewed and approved by someone other than its author before it's merged.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Tests and security scans run automatically in {{CI/CD: GitHub Actions}} on every change, and changes can't be deployed until required checks pass.
Evidence: Pipeline configuration; required checks; run history.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Production is separated from development and test environments.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Only authorised developers can deploy to production, and deployments run only through {{CI/CD: GitHub Actions}} from the protected branch.
Evidence: Deployer list; pipeline permissions; deployment history.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Production infrastructure is defined in {{infrastructure as code: Terraform}}, and infrastructure changes are peer reviewed before they're applied.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Security gates block deployment of changes with unresolved critical findings from code, dependency or secret scanning.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Access requests, changes, incidents and customer data requests are tracked in {{ticketing: Linear}}, recording each request, approval and resolution.
Evidence: Ticket history with approvals and resolution.
Policy: POL-11 Secure Development and Change Management Policy

What we do: Production data is backed up automatically with {{backups: Amazon RDS automated backups}}, and backups are encrypted, retained per the retention schedule and stored separately from production.
Policy: POL-13 Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy

What we do: A business continuity and disaster recovery plan sets out how the company responds to and recovers from disruption, and is reviewed at least annually.
Policy: POL-13 Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Policy

What we do: AI models and platforms in use, including {{AI tools: Claude / GitHub Copilot}}, are inventoried with an owner, purpose and the data shared, and are approved before use.
An AI acceptable use policy defines approved AI tools and what data personnel may enter into them.
Agreements with {{AI tools: Claude / GitHub Copilot}} prevent customer data from being used to train their models, and only the data needed is shared.

Code and configuration changes written with AI assistance, including {{AI tools: Claude / GitHub Copilot}}, are reviewed, tested and deployed by a person who takes responsibility for them through the standard change process.
Evidence: Pull requests showing human review and approval of AI-assisted changes.

What we do: Internal and external parties can report security concerns through published channels, and reports are triaged.
Evidence: Disclosure page; security inbox; triage log.

What we do: Service commitments, security responsibilities and customer responsibilities are communicated to customers through contracts, documentation or a trust centre, and customers are told when they change.
Customer-facing APIs authenticate and authorise every request and enforce rate limits, and customers can rotate or revoke their API keys.
Customers receive documented guidance on the security settings they control, such as users, multi-factor authentication and integrations.
